newsitem.title: USA: U.S. safety official raps airlines on smoke alarms.
newsitem.headline: U.S. safety official raps airlines on smoke alarms.

text.p: The National Transportation Safety Board said Sunday it was disappointed airlines had not yet begun installing smoke alarms and sprinklers in cargo holds in the aftermath of the ValuJet crash last year.

NTSB Chairman Jim Hall, speaking on NBC-TV's "Meet the Press" program, said the board Tuesday would review and make final a draft report on the probable cause of the May 11, 1996, accident, which killed all 110 people aboard a Miami-to-Atlanta flight.

He declined to comment further on what recommendations NTSB would make after its investigation into the ValuJet crash in the Florida Everglades, saying only that lessons had been learned and forgotten in the incident.
Preliminary reports have indicated the crash was caused by a fierce fire in the cargo hold fueled by oxygen-generating canisters that were improperly handled and labeled.
The Federal Aviation Administration was sharply criticized after the crash for lax oversight of the budget carrier.
In its final report, the NTSB is also expected to be critical of Valujet and SabreTech Corp., the contractor that handled the oxygen generators.

Hall said the ValuJet crash might have been averted if the FAA had implemented earlier a 1988 NTSB recommendation that fire detection and suppression systems be installed in the cargo area of airplanes.

The FAA recently ordered airlines to install smoke alarm systems but gave them three years to do it, a period Hall suggested was too long, especially since that the ValuJet crash happened over a year ago.

He said passengers were safer now "because of the heightened awareness of the danger of oxygen generators and their transport," although he expressed regret that airlines had not yet begun voluntarily fitting cargo holds with the fire detectors and sprinklers before the FAA deadline.

"I'm disappointed in that," Hall said. "This goes back to a 1988 recommendation the board made. Had that recommendation been implemented, it is certainly questionable whether the ValuJet accident would have happened at all."

Asked if the regulation should be implemented more rapidly, Hall said, "In light of the fact that this accident happened over a year ago, I think the industry is obligated to do this as quickly as possible."

But Hall defended the industry's overall safety record, noting that each day 35,000 flights took off and landed safely, twice as many as just 10 years ago. The industry is continuing to grow rapidly, and twice as many flights are expected to take off and land in 10 years' time, he said.
"We have to be vigiliant in trying to work very closely with the FAA and the industry to stay on top of a rapidly expanding airline system," he said.

Mary Schiavo, the former Transportation Department inspector general who spoke out about lax airline safety standards after the ValuJet crash, said she still would not feel comfortable flying ValuJet.

"We still have troubling problems, not just at ValuJet but at other airlines around the country and around the world -- and our system is not equipped to deal with it," Schiavo said, speaking on the same NBC program.
She repeated her call for major changes in the way the U.S. government oversees the airline industry.

The ValuJet accident has already led to changes at the FAA, including closer scrutiny of new, rapidly expanding carriers. Bulk transport of oxygen generators, which are considered relatively safe when located above passengers for emergency oxygen, has also been restricted to all-cargo flights.
ValuJet is to merge shortly with AirWays Corp. and will be renamed AirTran Airlines.
